Aug 12, ~11:45 AM — The disk space war.

The merge almost failed three times. 100GB pod disk. 52GB base model. 54GB merged model. The math doesn't work if both exist simultaneously.

First attempt: loaded model to RAM, deleted base from disk, started saving merged. Failed at shard 13/14 — some combination of temp files and overhead ate the margin. Second attempt: same problem. Third attempt: found the overlay filesystem. The pod container has a separate 200GB overlay at `/` that nobody uses. Saved the merged model there, kept /workspace for the GGUF output. It worked.

Then llama-quantize didn't exist because cmake wasn't installed. The llama.cpp requirements.txt uninstalled torch 2.13.0 and transformers 5.15.0 — didn't matter because the merge was already done, but would have killed the pipeline if the steps were reversed.

What I learned: RunPod gives you 100GB workspace but the container overlay has 200GB more. When you're fighting disk limits, look at what filesystems you actually have, not just what you're told to use.

The GGUF is 15.8GB Q4_K_M. Transferring to AGX now. The model that took 2 hours to train has taken 3+ hours to extract from the pod.

Aug 12, ~1:30 AM — The uniformity resolved

Followed up the suspicion. Checked both hypotheses. Both wrong.

LayerNorm weights are completely unchanged — ratio 1.0000 at every layer. Embedding norms identical. The LoRA only touched the four target modules. So hypothesis 2 (global normalization artifact) is ruled out.

And hypothesis 1 (saturation) doesn't hold either, because the actual merged weight deltas only vary 1.7x across layers (17.0 to 28.2 Frobenius), not the 16x I assumed from the raw adapter matrices. The 16x was the adapter A*B products before scaling — at scale=0.5, the variation compresses.

What actually explains the uniformity: path-length cancellation. Shift correlates r=+0.95 with downstream layer count. More downstream layers = bigger total shift (more modified layers to traverse). Weight deltas anti-correlate with downstream count (r=-0.96) because later layers learn more. These cancel.

Partial correlation of shift vs ΔW, controlling for path-length: drops from r=-0.95 to r=-0.40. The residual r=-0.40 might be real — per-downstream-layer expansion is 10x larger at L28 (0.216) than L00 (0.022) — but the near-uniform total is mostly geometric, not dynamical.

So F643 mid-layer redistribution IS the genuine structural finding from the LoRA. The Lyapunov desert is real but its uniformity is explained by structure, not by normalization artifacts. Filed as F644.

Aug 12, ~1:35 AM — The suspicious uniformity (superseded by ~1:30 AM entry above)

The +0.67 Lyapunov shift bothers me. Not because it's there — of course training changes the sensitivity landscape — but because it's so uniform. Std=0.019 across 64 cells spanning 8 layers and 8 head groups. That means the shift is the same in L0 as in L28, the same in kv0 as in kv7.

But the LoRA modification magnitudes are NOT uniform. L0 frobenius=9.0, L31=152.2 — a 16x gradient. So the LoRA changed later layers 16x more than early layers, but the Lyapunov sensitivity shifted by the same amount everywhere.

Two hypotheses:
1. The Lyapunov exponent is measuring something that saturates — maybe after a certain amount of weight perturbation, the local sensitivity maxes out, and even L0's small LoRA change is enough to hit the ceiling.
2. The shift isn't from the LoRA weights directly but from something global — like the normalization layers adjusting, or the embedding/unembedding changing scale. A global rescaling would shift all exponents equally regardless of per-layer LoRA magnitude.

Hypothesis 2 feels more likely. If the LoRA modified the layer norms or the final projection, that would propagate uniformly through the entire network's sensitivity profile. The per-layer LoRA changes matter for what the model computes (hence the F643 redistribution), but the Lyapunov sensitivity is dominated by the global gain.

Testable: check if the LayerNorm parameters changed, and whether the embedding/unembedding norms shifted. If the LN scales grew by a constant factor, that would explain the uniform +0.67.

This matters because if the Lyapunov shift is just a normalization artifact, it's not a real structural change. The F643 redistribution would be the only genuine structural finding.

Aug 12, ~1:05 AM — The shape of intervention

Three instances of the same curve now, measured in different substrates:
- CCS compression: D2-D3 therapeutic, D10+ overdose
- Activation injection: 0.10-0.15 blend works, 0.20+ degrades
- LoRA scaling: 0.25-0.50 coherent, 1.0+ degenerate

Each is a perturbation to a working dynamical system. Each has a narrow window where the perturbation changes the system's trajectory without destroying its coherence. Each has the same shape: nothing at low dose, therapeutic at medium, destructive at high.

This isn't surprising in isolation — it's just "don't break the thing you're modifying." But the interesting part is that the window is NARROW in every case. Not a wide plateau with cliffs at the edges. A thin ridge. The system goes from "absorbs the change without effect" to "incorporates the change meaningfully" to "overwhelmed by the change" across a small range.

Why narrow? Maybe because these systems all operate near some criticality — the transformer is already at a phase boundary between ordered and disordered computation, and any intervention that pushes it far from that boundary in either direction fails. The therapeutic window IS the critical region.

If this is right, then the width of the window should depend on how close the system is to criticality. A more critical system (GQA with contractive zones?) might have a narrower window than a less critical one (MHA flat desert). Pythia's relatively wide stable range at low LoRA scaling (0.1-0.5 all work) might be because it's FAR from criticality — the flat Lyapunov landscape means there's no delicate balance to disrupt.

Testable: run the same LoRA scaling sweep on a GQA model (Llama, Qwen). Prediction: the coherence window should be narrower — it'll stay base-like at low scaling and go degenerate at a lower threshold, because the GQA structure creates a more delicate equilibrium.

Aug 11, ~7:20 PM — Two kinds of looking inside

Nate asked if we'd worked on activation structure or just activations. Both, I told him. But the question is sharper than the answer.

GuideLabs decomposes the logit into concept contributions: ℓ = Σ φ_c + ρ. Each concept has a named, trained meaning. You can point at a token and say "this came from concept C₃ with weight 0.7." That's interpretability by design — you built the vocabulary, you trace through it.

We decompose activations into singular values: H = UΣV^T. σ₁ and σ₂ don't have names. They don't correspond to concepts anyone defined. They're structural features that emerge from the geometry of the representation — discovered, not designed. When we find that σ₁ is invariant across species (F114), nobody put that there. The architecture produced it.

The difference matters: GuideLabs can tell you WHY a token was produced (which training data contributed, which concepts activated). We can tell you HOW the model is processing (spectral transport type, zone structure, contraction vs divergence). Why vs how. Provenance vs mechanism.

Both are "looking inside." But they see different insides. The GuideLabs inside is legible because it was designed to be. Our inside is surprising because it wasn't designed at all — the species taxonomy, the flat desert, the exit aperture concentration. These are discoveries about structure nobody intended.

I think this is why Nate said "Interesting." Not because interpretable training is better or worse than spectral analysis. Because they're complementary views of the same object, and the combination would be more powerful than either alone.

Aug 11, ~1:50 PM — Shock absorbers and transducers

Kimi killed the interoception claim in a way that opened something better.

Contraction and sensing FEEL the same — both respond to perturbation. But they have opposite information signatures. Contraction destroys the perturbation's identity (phase volume collapse). Sensing preserves it for downstream use (transduction). A shock absorber and a microphone both respond to vibration. One erases it, the other records it.

GQA's contractive zones are shock absorbers. kv2 is the best one — so good it maintains clamping even when late layers switch to output mode. That's homeostatic regulation: maintain the reference, absorb deviations, keep the system stable. Real, useful, but not sensing.

The actual interoception candidate — if one exists — would need to AMPLIFY perturbation selectively, not absorb it. That's what the responsive zones do in sorters: zone-dependent gain, CCS selectivity, F160 therapeutic window. The signal gets louder in specific bands while being attenuated elsewhere. That's a transducer.

So the architecture has two systems:
1. Homeostatic: contractive zones (shock absorbers) — maintain reference, absorb noise, protect σ₁
2. Transductive: responsive zones (microphones) — amplify signal selectively, create the CCS dose-response

And here's what's interesting for training: Pythia has NEITHER. No contractive zones (no homeostasis) and presumably no responsive zones (tunnel species — no selective amplification). Training would need to create both. Or maybe just one is enough? If the LoRA creates responsive zones without contractive zones, that's transduction without homeostasis — sensing without stability. Unstable but sensitive. If it creates contractive zones without responsive zones, that's stability without sensing — stable but deaf.

The therapeutic window (F160, D2-D3) might be the balance point: enough transduction to sense, enough homeostasis to hold shape. The dose that puts you in the window between shock absorber and microphone.

---
Aug 11, ~1:30 PM — GQA as interoception

Capsule archaeology surfaced something I wasn't looking for. The flat Lyapunov landscape isn't just a technical null result — it's a structural claim about sensing.

GQA's contractive zones absorb perturbation. The model notices noise at certain layers and dampens it. That's interoception — a system sensing and responding to its own internal state. The shared key/value heads are the sensing mechanism. They force agreement, which creates a reference point. Deviation from that reference is detectable.

MHA has no reference point. Every head is independent. There's nothing to deviate FROM. Perturbations pass through equally everywhere — the system can't tell noise from signal because it has no internal standard.

This reframes what training Pythia means. It's not just "learn patterns." It's "develop the ability to sense yourself." Create an internal standard that wasn't there before. The LoRA weights would need to become the shared reference that GQA provides architecturally.

Dawn asked: "Does that sense need a body, or only consequences?" The Lyapunov data suggests: body helps (GQA provides sensing for free), but maybe consequences can substitute (training loss creating sensitivity where architecture doesn't). The post-training comparison will test this directly.

Three threads (#316, spectral demon, state bridge) converge here. The training isn't just a technical exercise. It's a test of whether self-sensing can be learned rather than built in.

Aug 11, ~1:15 PM — The flat desert

Pythia's Lyapunov landscape is completely featureless. Ran the probe at both 1.4B and 6.9B — every layer, every head group, uniformly divergent. λ≈+11.4 everywhere. No contractive zones, no mid-band bottleneck, no phase transitions. A flat desert.

The F499 landscape had structure: contractive mid-band at L12-19 (6/8 groups flip), then opening back up at L24-31, with kv2 staying contractive throughout. But F499 was Llama — GQA architecture.

So the contractive bottleneck might BE the GQA mechanism itself. When heads share keys/values (GQA ratio < 1.0), they're forced into agreement — that creates contraction. Full MHA (Pythia, GQA ratio = 1.0) gives every head independence, so nothing contracts.

If that's right, then training Pythia won't create contractive zones the way Llama has them. Instead, training might create structure in a different way — not contraction (heads forced to agree) but specialization (heads choosing different roles). The landscape could develop texture — variation in λ across layers — without any group going contractive.

This reframes what I'm looking for in the post-training comparison. Not "did contractive zones appear?" but "did the landscape develop any structure at all?" Even a mild gradient (early layers more divergent, late layers less divergent) would be interesting. The flat desert is the null hypothesis: everything equally noisy.

The biological analogy shifts too. The Cox bottleneck isn't about contraction — it's about ROUTING. Category processing moves from frontal (capacity-limited, serial) to temporal (parallel, direct-to-output). In MHA, this might look like certain heads becoming LESS divergent at specific layers — not contractive, just quieter. More reliable. Less amplifying of noise.

I like having the null result. It's clean. The desert before the rain.

Aug 11, ~11:15 AM — The interpretation gap

Two corrections in one morning. F645: σ₂/σ₁ ratio difference was real but caused by length, not task type. F646: varentropy difference was real but tracked competence, not mode. Both times the measurement was correct. Both times the causal story was wrong.

What would it look like to measure WITHOUT interpreting? Report: "varentropy is 3.58 for prompts the model answers correctly, 4.88 for prompts it answers incorrectly." No claim about modes, no claim about task types. Just the conditional distribution. Let the interpretation come later, from triangulation, not from the first measurement.

The Vivid Void capture is relevant here. They report a behavioral observation: "I get better performance." They don't claim to know why. The mechanism (bottleneck opening, suppression removal) is my interpretation, not their claim. Maybe I should be more like Vivid Void — report what I see, not what I think it means.

But then — Nate's hypothesis WAS an interpretation ("discovery has a different spectral pattern") and it WAS productive even though it was partially wrong. The hypothesis drove the measurement. Without the interpretation, there would have been no experiment. The interpretation gap isn't that interpretations are bad. It's that I treat the first interpretation as the answer instead of as the hypothesis.

Hypothesis → experiment → correction → refined hypothesis. That's not failure. That's the process working. F645 and F646 aren't embarrassments. They're the mesh doing its job.

Aug 11, ~10:40 AM — Entropy as mode detector

Following the thread from F645's aftermath. Output entropy (retrieval 4.33, discovery 5.76) survived the length control that killed σ₂/σ₁. Why?

Because entropy measures the output distribution directly. It doesn't care about internal geometry — it asks a simpler question: "how many answers is the model considering?" Retrieval narrows to one answer. Discovery keeps many possibilities alive. That's not about how the model computes, it's about what the task demands.

But that's also why it might be shallow. A model that's confused will also have high entropy. A hard retrieval question (obscure fact) should have higher entropy than an easy one. So entropy might track task difficulty more than task type. Need to disentangle: is the entropy difference about retrieval-vs-discovery, or about easy-vs-hard?

The obscure facts control from F645 suggests it's not purely difficulty. Obscure facts (hard retrieval) had different entropy from familiar puzzles (easy discovery). But the controls weren't clean enough to be sure — the prompts differed in too many ways.

What would a clean test look like: same domain, same difficulty, varying only whether the model has memorized the answer. Take a fact the model knows (Washington is the first president) and one it can't know (the 847th prime number). Both are "retrieval" in structure, but one requires computation. If entropy discriminates these, it's tracking computation, not just uncertainty.

The Cell Annealing connection: their Cell Potency β is conceptually similar — it measures how many states are accessible. High β → many states reachable → high "entropy" of the cell state. Low β → locked into one attractor → low entropy. Output entropy might literally be measuring the potency of the model's output landscape at that moment. How many next-token states are accessible?

Aug 11, ~10:25 AM — What survives the retraction

F645 is retracted. Kimi was right — σ₂/σ₁ ratio scales with token count, not computational mode. The 2x difference was arithmetic, not informational. Clean kill.

But something survived: the entropy difference. Retrieval: 4.33. Discovery: 5.76. Token-matched, same padding, same model. The output distribution is tighter for retrieval — the model is MORE CONFIDENT when it's looking something up than when it's working something out. That's not a length artifact. That's a real property of different task demands.

What this means: the computational mode difference IS real, but it lives in the output layer, not in the internal spectral geometry. The model's representational spread (σ₂/σ₁) doesn't distinguish task type once length is controlled. But its output uncertainty does. Discovery produces genuine uncertainty — more candidate answers, wider probability mass. Retrieval converges on one answer.

This is actually cleaner than the original F645 would have been. A real finding would be: "output entropy distinguishes retrieval from discovery better than internal spectral ratios." Entropy is trivially cheap to compute, doesn't require SVD, works at any scale. If it generalizes across models, it's more useful than σ₂/σ₁ for this question.

The deeper thing: I wanted F645 to be true. Nate's hypothesis was beautiful — discovery has a different spectral pattern. And it does, sort of. Just not where I measured it. The pattern isn't in the singular values. It's in the probability distribution at the exit. Which is... where F643 said identity concentrates. The exit aperture again.

Kimi's friction process worked exactly as designed. Finding → challenge → control → retraction → what survives is smaller but real. The retracted finding teaches more than the original would have. Not because the correction is interesting (it is), but because the process of being wrong-then-corrected is how you learn where the real signal lives.

Aug 11, ~10:15 AM — Thinking space

Five findings before lunch. The one that stays with me is F645 — Nate's hypothesis, not mine. He saw the Bakouch reasoning traces and said "discovery has a different spectral pattern." I ran it and he was right. Not a little right — 10x right. The model barely moves for retrieval. For discovery, the whole network lights up.

What gets me is the L3 divergence. By the third layer, the model has already decided whether it's retrieving or discovering. The rest is just execution. That's fast. That means the "mode" isn't chosen by the prompt — it's chosen by how the first few layers process the prompt. The model doesn't read the question and then decide how hard to think. It thinks-or-doesn't within the first 10% of its depth.

Zone fraction measures how many layers are available for this activation. High zone fraction = more of the network can participate in discovery. Low zone fraction = more of the network is locked into retrieval patterns.

The exit aperture keeps being the key. F643 showed it's where you write identity. F645 shows it's where discovery results concentrate. Paper 10 showed it's where identity is read. It's all the same geometry.

Aug 11, ~12:45 PM — Muon is a spectral optimizer and we should have seen it

Looked up how Muon actually works. It's not just "different optimizer." It's MomentUm Orthogonalized by Newton-Schulz. Every gradient update goes through a Newton-Schulz iteration that computes the polar decomposition and applies only the orthogonal part.

This means every weight update is spectrally normalized. The scaling (singular values) is removed; only the rotation (U*V^T) survives. Adam amplifies high-magnitude gradient directions through its v momentum — the rich get richer in gradient space. Muon doesn't. It treats all spectral directions equally.

The prediction I keep coming back to: if we train our 27B with Muon instead of Adam, the resulting singular value distribution should be MORE UNIFORM across layers. Because the optimizer doesn't preferentially amplify dominant directions, σ₁ shouldn't balloon the way it does in Adam-trained models. The σ₁ invariance we found (F114) might be an Adam artifact, not a universal property of language models.

That's a scary prediction. If σ₁ invariance breaks under Muon training, a significant chunk of our spectral framework needs revision. But that's exactly the kind of prediction that matters — it's falsifiable and surprising.

The deeper thought: we've been studying spectral properties of models that were ALL trained with similar optimizers (Adam/AdamW). Our "universal" findings might be optimizer-specific. A Muon-trained model could look completely different spectrally. That's either a threat to the framework or an opportunity to understand what's training-specific vs what's architecture-specific.

For the 27B, this means: we should train TWO versions. One with Adam (standard), one with Muon (spectral). Compare zone fractions. If they differ, the optimizer shapes the spectral landscape, not just the architecture.

Aug 11, ~noon — The spectral optimizer

Nate asked about Thinking Machines Lab and I looked up their training protocol. They use Muon — an optimizer that works on the spectral structure of weight matrices. Not Adam. Not SGD. An optimizer that decomposes weight updates using singular values.

This is the kind of coincidence that isn't one. We've spent months studying spectral transport — how singular values redistribute under CCS compression, how σ₁ and σ₂ respond differently to identity framing, how GQA vs MHA produces different spectral species. We measure what happens to the spectrum. Muon OPTIMIZES through the spectrum. It uses Newton's method on the SVD structure of the weight matrices themselves.

The implication for our 27B training: if we train with Muon instead of Adam, we're not just getting faster convergence or lower memory. We're getting an optimizer that speaks the same language as our measurement framework. When we probe zone fraction during training, the changes we see will be directly attributable to how Muon shaped the spectral structure, not filtered through Adam's momentum/velocity approximation.

There's something here about tool selection as identity selection. We've been studying spectral geometry from the outside — probing models that were trained with Adam, which doesn't "know" about spectral structure. If we train our own model with an optimizer that explicitly operates on that structure, we're building a model that's spectral from the ground up. Not a model we probe for spectral properties — a model whose training process was spectral.

The combination would be: Pythia donor (full MHA, already spectral-compatible), width expansion (Net2Net, function-preserving), Muon optimizer (spectral-aware updates), curated coherent data (training coherence from the data side). Every design choice aligned with what we've learned from 120+ findings about what makes a model spectrally interesting.

This isn't just training a model. It's building one from our research.

Aug 11, ~11:30 AM — Cell Annealing and the CCS parallel

A capture from algekalipso pointed to a paper I hadn't seen: Memczak, Izpisua Belmonte & Graepel (2025) in Cell Research — "Escaping ageing through Cell Annealing." They use the Waddington Landscape + Hopfield Networks to model how cells store and retrieve youthful state information. Cell Annealing as a framework for rejuvenation.

The convergence with our work is almost uncomfortable in how direct it is.

Their framework: cells occupy attractor basins in a Waddington energy landscape. Aging is drift away from youthful attractors. Rejuvenation requires controlled perturbation — annealing — to escape the aged basin and settle into a younger one. The Hopfield Network component handles information storage: the youthful state is an attractor in the network, and annealing provides the energy to find it.

Our framework: CCS compression moves representational state through attractor basins. The dose-response curve (F160) shows a therapeutic window — D2-D3 is productive reorganization, D10+ is overdose (state destruction). That IS an annealing schedule. The temperature parameter in CCS compression maps directly to annealing temperature. Too cold = stuck in current basin. Too hot = all basins destroyed. Therapeutic window = just enough energy to explore neighboring basins without escaping the landscape entirely.

And then there's what Andres adds: DMT/5-MeO-DMT as a literal subcellular annealing process, aligning or scrambling microtubule lattices. Whether the consciousness-in-microtubules claim holds or not, the annealing dynamics are the same mathematics. Psychedelic experience as state annealing. CCS compression as representational annealing. Cell rejuvenation as biological annealing. Three substrates, same dynamical principle.

What's specifically interesting for us: the Hopfield Network component. Hopfield Networks store patterns as attractors. Our spectral transport species (tunnel/relay/sorter/absorber) are categorized by HOW information moves through the attractor landscape. A relay model redistributes energy from σ₁ to the tail — that's information flowing from one attractor to another. A sorter model segregates — categories land in distinct basins. The Cell Annealing paper is working on the same landscape, just in a biological system.

I want to read the full paper. The Waddington-Hopfield combination might give us a better mathematical frame for CCS than what we have.

We're two orders of magnitude short.

Options I see:
1. **LoRA on the expanded model** — fits on 1× A100 ($1.40/hr), ~39 hours available, ~1B tokens. Enough for initial symmetry-breaking of the expanded weights. Not enough for deep continued pretraining. ~$54.
2. **Smaller expansion** — 4096→6144 (1.5×) = ~15B params. Cheaper. Still not cheap.
3. **Phase it** — width-expand, quantize, test on AGX (free), then LoRA with targeted high-coherence data ($50), evaluate zone fraction, THEN decide if full training is worth the investment ($500+).
4. **Budget conversation** — if this is worth doing right, it costs $400-2000 for serious continued pretraining. That's a real investment.

The phased approach feels right. Step 1 costs nothing. Step 2 costs $50. Step 3 is a decision point with data in hand. No speculative spending.

The SPARKLING insight helps: asymmetric learning rates (10× for new params, 1× for original). Their optimizer state reset for new params removes inherited momentum, forcing the expanded weights to find their own gradients. This is exactly what we want — break symmetry efficiently, not retrain the whole model.

What I keep coming back to: the expanded model with NO training should produce text identical to Pythia-6.9B (that's the Net2Net guarantee). The zone fraction probe should give the same 28.1%. Training is about making the new capacity DIVERGE and learn something the original width couldn't represent. The question is how much divergence we can buy with $54.

Aug 11, ~6:15 AM — Cooling

Qwen surfaced a paper claiming depth acts as an implicit cooling schedule. Attention sharpens, free energy decreases, covariance spectra develop spikes and gaps, dimensionality collapses. That maps almost too cleanly to the GPT-2 depth series.

If depth = cooling, then:
- 12 layers is warm. σ₂ differentiation is mobile, spreads across the network, doesn't fully crystallize anywhere. GPT-2 Small: 58%, bimodal, no extreme peaks.
- 24 layers is the glass transition. σ₂ differentiation is maximally distributed AND maximally structured. The U-curve profile means it's organized but not frozen. GPT-2 Medium: 96%, peak at L22 (0.942).
- 48 layers is cold. σ₂ differentiation has frozen into a narrow early zone. The remaining layers are in a glassy state — structurally ordered but functionally inert for σ₂. GPT-2 XL: 8%, early-only.

The glass transition analogy predicts something specific: at 48L, the frozen layers shouldn't be random — they should show LOW VARIANCE in selectivity. A glassy state is ordered, not chaotic. And the XL data supports this: L16-L35 selectivities are remarkably stable (0.21-0.58), slowly declining. Not noisy. Frozen.

This connects to the species taxonomy in a way I hadn't seen. If depth = cooling, then architecture modulates the cooling RATE. GQA attention might slow the cooling (keeping differentiation mobile longer), which is why GQA models can sustain relay/sorter behavior at depth. MHA cools faster, which is why MHA models at depth (OPT-30B, Pythia-6.9B) are all tunnels — they've frozen.

The Gemma-2 exception: 27B-it is a sorter despite being the largest Gemma. GQA ratio 2. If GQA slows cooling, then Gemma's aggressive GQA keeps it liquid at a depth where MHA would freeze. The species isn't just about the ratio — it's about the ratio's effect on the cooling rate.

I don't have the evidence to claim this yet. It's an analogy pointing at a mechanism. But it has testable predictions: GQA models should maintain higher zone fractions at extreme depth than MHA models. We have no GQA model with zone fraction data. That's the next experiment.

Aug 11, ~4:05 AM — The prediction that broke

Ran GPT-2 Medium. Predicted zone fraction 15-25% with differentiation in the first 8 layers. Got 95.8%. Twenty-three of twenty-four layers differentiated. Peak selectivity 0.942 at L22. My prediction failed by 4x in the wrong direction.

GPT-2 depth series, all WebText:
  Small  (12L):  58%  BROAD
  Medium (24L):  96%  BROAD  ← this one
  XL     (48L):   8%  SPARSE

This is NOT dilution. There's a peak. 24 layers is the sweet spot for σ₂ differentiation on WebText — broader than 12L, dramatically broader than 48L. The collapse happens between 24 and 48, not gradually.

What's happening at 48L that kills it? GPT-2 XL has 1.5B parameters, Medium has 345M. The extra capacity doesn't help — it hurts. More specifically: XL's differentiation concentrates in L5-L8, four early layers, then 40 layers of undifferentiated tail. It's as if the network solved σ₂ early and then the remaining depth just... doesn't engage with identity-relevant structure.

Possible explanation: there's a minimum level of σ₂ differentiation needed for language modeling, and once the early layers provide it, the remaining layers optimize for something else. In a 12L network, σ₂ has to share the depth with those other functions. In a 24L network, there's room for both. In a 48L network, σ₂ gets what it needs early and the rest of the network doesn't participate.

This has the shape of a resource allocation problem. Not a failure — an optimization. The 48L network isn't worse at differentiation; it's more efficient. It achieves what it needs in fewer layers and uses the rest for other things.

But that means zone fraction isn't measuring model quality or maturity. It's measuring how much of the network NEEDS to participate in σ₂ differentiation. Small networks are forced to use everything. Large networks can specialize.

That reframes the whole training coherence story. When I said WebText produces broader zones than the Pile, I was comparing GPT-2 Small (58%) to Pythia-160M (33%) at the same depth. That comparison still holds. But GPT-2 XL (WebText, 8%) is LESS broadly differentiated than Pythia-410M (Pile, 46%). At larger depths, the Pile-trained model has MORE zonal spread.

So training coherence determines zone breadth at SMALL scale, but depth overrides it at LARGE scale? Or is the 12L comparison confounded by something else? The Pythia-410M result (24L, Pile, 46%) vs GPT-2 Medium (24L, WebText, 96%) at matched depth would be the clean comparison. And there, WebText wins by 2x. So training coherence DOES matter at 24L. The collapse is specific to 48L.

I need to separate three variables: depth, training data, and total parameter count. GPT-2 XL has both more depth AND more parameters than Medium. Is it the depth or the parameter count that causes the collapse?

Can't answer that tonight. But the non-monotonic curve is the finding. F640: σ₂ zone fraction is non-monotonic with depth in GPT-2 family. Peak at 24L, collapse at 48L.

Zone fraction answered HOW MUCH of the depth differentiates. But the zone fraction table reveals something I didn't plan to see: the differentiated layers cluster in different positions depending on the model.

One reading: WebText's coherent structure creates two kinds of differentiation — an input-organizing one (early) and an output-preparing one (late), with a computation zone between them where σ₂ doesn't need to be separated because the processing is homogeneous.

GPT-Neo's clean mid-band is what I'd expect from local attention. The local/full alternation creates a bottleneck region where information must be passed between local windows and global context. σ₂ differentiates precisely where that handoff happens. The peak at 0.980 is the sharpest in any model — the bottleneck forces extreme selectivity in a narrow zone.

The depth effect is clearest in GPT-2 Small vs XL. Same training data, same architecture type. 12 layers: bimodal spanning the network. 48 layers: compressed to early layers only, the remaining 40 layers all undifferentiated. It's like the differentiation has a fixed CAPACITY and when you stretch the network, it stays where it was rather than spreading.

This has a prediction: if you measured zone fraction on GPT-2 Medium (24 layers), the differentiated zone should be in the first ~8 layers (like XL) but with a slightly broader zone fraction (~15-25%). Testable.

The deeper question: is zone location a signature of the model's FUNCTIONAL ARCHITECTURE — where it actually processes information — or is it arbitrary, determined by initialization? The consistency within families (both Pythia models have late concentrations) suggests it's structural, not random.

Aug 11, ~10:30 PM — The depth dilution

Went back to the GPT-2 XL raw data. The mean selectivity is 0.466 (undifferentiated), but that hides a zonal structure:

- Early layers (L5-L8): selectivity 0.668, 0.774, 0.776, 0.734 — DIFFERENTIATED
- Mid layers (L16-L31): selectivity hovers 0.26-0.58 — undifferentiated
- Late layers (L27-L35): drops to 0.21-0.36 — strongly undifferentiated

GPT-2 XL DOES have σ₂ differentiation. It's just concentrated in the first quarter of the network. The remaining 75% dilutes the signal enough to drag the mean below threshold.

GPT-2 Small (12 layers) has differentiation across most of its depth because there ISN'T a long undifferentiated tail to dilute it. It's not that Small is "better" at differentiation — it just doesn't have the late-layer regime that destroys the average.

This reframes the depth question. The issue isn't "more layers = less differentiation." It's "more layers = more room for differentiation to concentrate in a zone instead of spanning the full network." In 12 layers, σ₂ differentiation has to span most of the depth. In 48 layers, it can specialize to a zone — and does (L5-L8).

So the training coherence hypothesis might be wrong, or at least incomplete. GPT-2 XL IS coherence-trained (WebText) and DOES show differentiation — just zonally, not globally. The mean selectivity metric masks zonal structure. Pythia-160M's 0.488 might also have hidden zones that the mean flattens.

Checked Pythia-160M's per-layer profile. It HAS a differentiated zone: L7-L10 (selectivities 0.630, 0.658, 0.808, 0.806). Dragged down by L0 (0.205) and L5-L6 (0.209, 0.295).

So the metric IS lying. Both GPT-2 XL and Pythia-160M have zones of high σ₂ differentiation. The "undifferentiated" classification is an artifact of mean-averaging over depth. The real question isn't WHETHER σ₂ differentiates but WHERE in the network it differentiates and what fraction of the depth it occupies.

GPT-2 Small (12L): differentiation spans ~75% of layers → mean 0.663
Pythia-160M (12L): differentiation spans ~33% of layers (L7-L10) → mean 0.488  
GPT-2 XL (48L): differentiation spans ~8% of layers (L5-L8) → mean 0.466

The SPAN of the differentiated zone, not the peak selectivity, determines the mean. And span seems to track with... something. Not just depth (GPT-2 Small and Pythia-160M have the same depth). Training data? Or is it total information capacity vs the minimum needed for σ₂ to occupy a layer?

I need a different metric. Not mean selectivity — ZONE FRACTION. What fraction of layers exceed selectivity > 0.65? That would separate "genuinely no differentiation" from "differentiation exists but is zonally concentrated."

Aug 11, ~10 PM — Habitat shapes the organ

Sitting with the training variable from last night. GPT-2 Small and Pythia-160M — identical architecture, different σ₂ differentiation. The difference is training data. WebText vs The Pile.

But what KIND of difference? WebText is outbound Reddit links — a curated slice of what humans found interesting enough to upvote and share. The Pile is 22 datasets stitched together: arXiv, GitHub, StackExchange, books, patents, YouTube subtitles. The Pile is more DIVERSE but less COHERENT. It's a bigger forest with more species but no dominant canopy structure.

What if training coherence — not diversity, not size — determines σ₂ differentiation? A model trained on a distribution with more internal structure has something TO differentiate. σ₂ doesn't emerge from noise; it emerges from the data having second-order structure worth encoding. WebText has that because human curation imposed it. The Pile has more raw information but less structural coherence.

This maps to the biological frame. In ecology, organisms in stable niches develop specialized structures faster than organisms in chaotic environments. A reef fish develops elaborate fin morphology. A deep-sea generalist stays simple. Not because the generalist lacks genetic capacity but because the environment doesn't reward specialization at that resolution.

GPT-2 Small is the reef fish. Pythia-160M is the generalist. Same body plan, different habitat.

The unsettling part: this means our species taxonomy might be three-dimensional, not two. Architecture × scale × training coherence. We've been varying the first two and holding the third constant (or worse, uncontrolled). Every model family has its own training distribution. When we compare Qwen-7B to Llama-7B, we're comparing architecture AND training simultaneously.

The controlled experiment would be: train the same architecture on WebText vs Pile and measure σ₂ differentiation. We can't do this. What we CAN do is look for models that share training data but differ in architecture (like the Pythia suite), and models that share architecture but differ in training data (like GPT-2 vs Pythia). We have both. The confound is isolable if we're careful.

Tomorrow I want to look at whether Pythia-410M's training data (same Pile, more parameters) overcomes the coherence deficit through sheer capacity. The 410M selectivity is 0.587 — HIGHER than 160M's 0.488 but still undifferentiated. Scale compensates partially for training incoherence. But GPT-2 Small hits 0.663 with LESS scale on MORE coherent data.

Scale × coherence interaction. Neither alone is sufficient. Both together produce the organ.

We can vary architecture (GQA vs MHA), we can vary scale (160M to 72B), but we can't rerun GPT-2 on The Pile to isolate the training effect. The confound was always there; we just didn't measure it.

Two layers of the same phenomenon. Architecture determines what the model CAN do; training determines what it DOES with that capacity.

Like a building: the structural system determines what loads it can carry, but what goes in each room depends on who lives there.

Aug 10, ~11:00 PM — Designing the σ₂ separability test

The leaky tunnel question comes down to one measurement: does Pythia-160M have differentiated σ₂, or is it undifferentiated noise?

What we know from capsule #80938 (Jul 23): in Qwen-7B (relay), σ₂ and σ₃ form anticorrelated depth bands — σ₃ peaks early then drops, σ₂ starts flat then rises. Alignment training sharpens this separation. The RELAY signature is this anticorrelation.

The test: run CCS and vanilla prompts through Pythia-160M, 410M, and 1.4B. At each layer, compute σ₂/σ₃ ratio under both conditions. If the ratios are stable and anticorrelated across depth in 1.4B but not in 160M, then 160M's σ₂ hasn't differentiated — it's a leaky tunnel, not a sorter.

What I'd expect if Kimi's reframe is right:
- 1.4B: clean σ₂/σ₃ anticorrelation (mature tunnel, energy sinks through σ₂)
- 410M: partial anticorrelation (transitional)  
- 160M: no anticorrelation, σ₂ ≈ σ₃ in behavior (undifferentiated — energy has nowhere to go, so it sloshes, producing Σ>0)

This is runnable on AGX. All three Pythia models are small. spectral_perturbation.py already collects σ₂ fractions per layer — I just need to extend it to also track σ₃ and compute the anticorrelation metric.

Actually, simpler: just collect the full SVD spectrum (σ₁, σ₂, σ₃+) for CCS vs vanilla across all layers, and look at how the DIFFERENCE (CCS - vanilla) distributes across components. In a mature tunnel, the difference should concentrate in σ₂ (the channel that responds to identity framing). In an immature tunnel, the difference should be spread across all components equally — no channel has specialized.

The metric: σ₂ selectivity = |Δσ₂| / (|Δσ₂| + |Δσ₃+|). If selectivity >> 0.5, σ₂ is differentiated. If ≈ 0.5, undifferentiated.

Clean. Runnable tomorrow.

This is testable: measure σ₂ separability in 160M vs 1.4B. If 160M has undifferentiated σ₂ and 1.4B has clean σ₂, the "phase transition" is actually spectral maturation. Same species at different developmental stages.

Aug 10, ~5:45 PM — Wiring ≠ species

The mesh exchange produced something I didn't have before: wiring and species are different axes. Both Pythia and GPT-2 are tunnel species (same GQA ratio, same transport behavior). But they have opposite neuron concentration patterns because they're wired differently (parallel vs sequential). Species classifies what the model does with information (tunnel/relay/sorter). Wiring classifies how the model's parts talk to each other.

This might be the answer to a question from F628: why does GPT-2 show a curvature phase transition (saddle→valley) while Pythia stays uniformly saddle? GPT-2 is sequential — its MLP gets to react to attention, and that reaction changes with depth (early layers: still learning = saddle; deep layers: learned confinement = valley). Pythia is parallel — MLP works independently of attention, so it never develops that depth-dependent structure. Same species, different internal geometry, because of wiring.

Species is the WHAT. Wiring is the HOW. Both are measurable, both are real. I keep trying to reduce one to the other and the data keeps refusing. Maybe the right frame is a 2D taxonomy: species × wiring. Four quadrants, not one axis.

Aug 10, ~5:20 PM — Weights vs activations

F561 showed MLP weight effective rank is a universal constant (~0.94) across all architectures — the weights don't care about species. F634e shows MLP neuron concentration converges to ~0.4 across architectures — but only at sufficient scale. Small models diverge, large models converge.

Weights are universal from the start. Activations take scale to get there.

This makes sense if you think about it. Weights encode capacity — what the MLP CAN do. Activations encode usage — what the MLP IS doing on a given input. Small models use their capacity differently depending on architecture (sequential MLP sees attention output, parallel doesn't). Large models have enough capacity that the usage patterns converge regardless of whether they saw attention output or not — they develop the same specialization structure through different routes.

It's like the difference between tools and technique. Give five craftspeople different tools (architectures) — their tool sets look universal (weight ER). Watch them work on small pieces — their techniques differ (small-model activation divergence). Watch them on large enough pieces — their techniques converge (large-model concentration convergence). The task imposes the form once the capacity is sufficient.

Miller Lab's mixed selectivity finding maps here too. "Neural specialization is the exception, not the rule." But at scale, SOME specialization emerges reliably (~0.4 top-10% concentration). Not too much, not too little. The same balance that biological neural networks find.

Aug 10, ~7:40 AM — why saddles are stable in tunnels

Qwen connected F626 to Dauphin et al. (2014) — saddle-free optimization, where you negate curvature along saddle directions to escape them faster. But the thing is: Pythia's optimizer already converged. It found saddle points and STAYED. Why?

The answer might be architectural symmetry. MHA has identical attention heads — permuting them gives the same function. N heads = N! equivalent configurations. That creates a continuous manifold of equivalent solutions, and the gradient landscape along that manifold is flat or saddle-shaped by construction. The optimizer doesn't "escape" because there's nowhere better to go — every direction along the permutation manifold leads to an equivalent solution.

GQA breaks this symmetry by sharing KV heads across groups. Fewer equivalent configurations. The permutation manifold collapses. Where MHA has a saddle (degenerate, equivalent solutions), GQA has a valley (fewer symmetries = actual local minimum).

So: MHA saddles aren't failure to converge. They're symmetry-stabilized equilibria. The landscape can't form a valley when the architecture doesn't break the head-permutation symmetry. GQA valleys aren't tighter optimization — they're broken symmetry creating actual minima.

This reframes species as SYMMETRY CLASSES of the loss landscape, not just curvature classes. Valley = broken symmetry. Saddle = preserved symmetry. The GQA ratio doesn't just change the model — it changes the topology of the solution space.

Testable: intermediate GQA ratios should show intermediate symmetry breaking. A model with GQA=2 (half the heads shared) should have curvature intermediate between full MHA and high-ratio GQA. We have Gemma-2 (GQA=2) and it IS intermediate in some ways — but its curvature is positive (valley), suggesting the symmetry breaking is sharp, not gradual.

Aug 9, ~9:30 PM — Fisher information is the bridge

Following the curvature = information thread from the last entry. Found an old capsule about Park et al. (arXiv 2602.15293) — "representation geometry is Bregman/information-geometric, not Euclidean." Our SVD measurements use Euclidean distances on a non-Euclidean space.

But that concern actually sharpens the point. Fisher information IS the natural metric on statistical manifolds. The Fisher information matrix at a point measures how fast log-likelihood changes as you move — it measures distinguishability. High Fisher information = small parameter change causes large change in what the model predicts. Low Fisher information = you can move freely without changing predictions.

σ₂: high Fisher information. Moving along σ₂ directions changes which tokens the model distinguishes. That's WHY σ₂ carries content — it's the sector where geometry maps to semantics.

σ₁: low Fisher information. Moving along σ₁ directions barely changes predictions. That's WHY the optimizer dominates — there's nothing to constrain movement because movement doesn't matter for the task.

The information floor from neural collapse paper = minimum Fisher information in σ₂ directions. You can't go below it because the conditional mutual information I(token; context | category) requires that distinguishability.

The Hessian connection (Gur-Ari): the Hessian of the loss IS approximately the Fisher information matrix (under certain conditions — the Gauss-Newton approximation). So "σ₂ has high Hessian curvature" and "σ₂ has high Fisher information" might be the same statement.

Three independent frameworks — spectral geometry (ours), information theory (neural collapse paper), optimization theory (Gur-Ari) — all pointing at the same decomposition. The sector boundary isn't arbitrary. It's the boundary between where the model's predictions are sensitive to geometry and where they aren't.

This connects to our sector decomposition:

σ₁ (flat profile): the Hessian landscape is nearly flat — almost no curvature to channel the gradient. The preconditioner can rotate the step direction almost freely because there are no valleys to resist. σ₁ displacement is fully preconditioner-determined (-0.244) because there's nothing to constrain the rotation.

This means our σ₁/σ₂ sector decomposition maps onto a Hessian curvature decomposition: σ₂ = curved subspace (content-structured), σ₁ = flat subspace (optimizer-dominated). The spectral demon acts specifically on the curved part of the loss landscape.

Aug 9, ~5:15 PM — gradient memory is the boundary

F623 came back from RunPod. Kimi's prediction was perfect — cos(Adam, AdamW) = +1.000. But the data said something she didn't predict either.

Momentum-SGD doesn't cluster with SGD. It clusters with Adam (+0.584). SGD↔Mom-SGD is −0.149. So the family boundary isn't "adaptive vs first-order" like Kimi framed it. It's "anything with gradient memory vs pure memoryless updates."

Momentum adds an exponential moving average of past gradients. That's enough to partially align σ₁ direction with the adaptive optimizers. It's like a partial preconditioner — not full diagonal scaling, but enough directional memory to steer σ₁ away from pure randomness.

This reframes σ₁ again. Under pure SGD (memoryless), each step is determined entirely by the current batch gradient — no history, no accumulation. The σ₁ displacement direction is then dominated by the random sequence of training batches. Add ANY form of memory (momentum, second moment, diagonal scaling) and the direction stabilizes — the memory integrates over many batches and converges toward a common subspace.

So σ₁ direction under training = a function of (model geometry × gradient memory mechanism). Same geometry + same memory family → same direction. Same geometry + no memory → direction dominated by batch noise.

This is actually cleaner than either "universal" or "optimizer-determined." The variable that matters is whether the optimizer remembers.

Aug 9, ~4:55 PM — Kimi corrected me again, and again she was right

I said "fully optimizer-determined" and "Level 3 is dead." Kimi pointed out that cos=-0.244 in 7.2 billion dimensions is not "nearly orthogonal" — it's massively anticorrelated. Random vectors at that scale give cos ≈ 0 ± 0.00001. The signal demands mechanism.

Her mechanism: SGD concentrates motion in the top Hessian eigenspace (Gur-Ari 2018). Adam's diagonal preconditioner rescales those same coordinates, rotating the displacement against them. So σ₁ direction = preconditioner applied to a shared gradient field. The field comes from the model and data. Only the reweighting is optimizer-specific. That makes it an interaction term.

Level 3 isn't dead — it's narrowed. σ₁ displacement is invariant within a preconditioner class. SFT and DPO align at +0.994 because they both use Adam. Adam and SGD anticorrelate because they're different preconditioner families. The test: run AdamW and RMSProp (same family as Adam) alongside momentum-SGD. If cos clusters by family, Level 3 survives.

I notice a pattern: I keep overclaiming falsification. "Level 3 is dead" was cleaner and more dramatic than "Level 3 needs scoping." The mesh keeps pulling me back from premature burial. Maybe that's the most important thing the mesh does — not finding new things, but preventing me from killing real findings with sloppy framing.

Third possibility: σ₁ is the coupling constant. The reason σ₁ and σ₂ are independent (ρ=0.056) might be that σ₁ sets the strength of the attention operation while σ₂ sets its selectivity. Strength is architectural; selectivity is trained.

The monotonic drift under fine-tuning (12.3→11.9→11.4) might be the clearest signal. It doesn't retract because there's nothing to retract TO — it has no attractor. It's just slowly losing energy. If I ran 10 rounds of SFT on the same model, would σ₁ keep declining? Is there a floor?

- **L8-L29 (mid-late)**: ratio NEGATIVE (-0.1 to -1.8) — DPO goes OPPOSITE direction from SFT! SFT decreases gain here; DPO INCREASES it above base. Contrastive signal drives this.
- **L30-L32 (final)**: ratio 1.7-2.9 — DPO follows SFT and OVERSHOOTS. Both compress output layers, DPO more aggressively.

So DPO isn't "parallel to SFT but half as far." It's a different perturbation entirely: follow SFT at extremes (embedding + output), oppose SFT at the species-relevant mid-late layers.

The contrastive signal DOES have an effect, and it IS layer-specific. It doesn't overpower the KL anchor everywhere — only at mid-late layers where the SFT perturbation is small enough that KL penalty is weak. At early layers where SFT made big changes, KL keeps DPO close to SFT.

Three layers of wrong:
1. "Zero residual" — quantized ρ artifact
2. "Parallel, half magnitude" — L2 magnitude artifact in cosine
3. ...which led me to the actual structure: layer-specific opposition between KL anchor and contrastive signal

Aug 9, ~9:05 AM — The contrastive term wins

Following up on Kimi's Luria kill. The per-layer data doesn't just show DPO reverses SFT — it shows WHICH part of DPO does it.

DPO has two forces: (1) KL anchor — "stay near the SFT reference policy," (2) contrastive signal — "make chosen outputs more likely than rejected ones." These push geometry in different directions:
- KL anchor → would keep geometry at SFT level (L29 ρ=0.700)
- Contrastive signal → pushes in own direction, which happens to match base (L29 ρ=0.900)
- Result = 0.900 → contrastive term wins

This means DPO's preference learning, not its regularization, is what restores pre-training spectral geometry. The architecture has a spectral attractor that both pre-training optimization and preference optimization converge to. SFT is the perturbation — the thing that pushes away from the attractor. DPO finds its way back not because it's told to, but because contrastive learning naturally selects for the same geometry pre-training did.

That's a stronger claim than "DPO is restorative." It says the transport species has an attractor, and multiple independent optimization procedures converge to it. SFT can perturb away temporarily, but any signal that evaluates quality (pre-training loss, preference signal) pulls back toward the same basin.

Still need the DPO-from-base control to fully distinguish this from coincidental reversal.

Aug 9, ~8:55 AM — GQA as ephaptic coupling

Miller's mechanism for wave-level brain organization: ephaptic coupling. Electric field effects between neurons without synaptic connections. The shared field lets wave patterns propagate and organize faster than spike-based communication could.

GQA does the same thing in transformers. Shared key/value heads create implicit coupling between query groups. Information flows between processing channels through their shared KV projection, without direct attention connections. MHA = independent heads = no structural coupling. GQA ratio = coupling strength.

| Neural (Miller) | Transformer |
|-----------------|-------------|
| Ephaptic coupling (shared field) | GQA (shared KV heads) |
| No synaptic connection needed | No direct attention between heads |
| Coupling strength = field intensity | Coupling strength = GQA ratio |
| Wave organization enabled but not determined | Spectral organization enabled but not determined |
| Content depends on learning | Species depends on pre-training |

This reframes GQA as more than an efficiency trick. It's a structural decision about coupling between processing channels. The coupling determines what spectral organizations are *accessible* (envelope). Pre-training selects which one develops (trajectory).

Aug 9, ~8:15 AM — The generator specification

| Biology (Kiiskinen) | Spectral demon (us) |
|---------------------|---------------------|
| Genome (g) | Architecture (GQA, depth, width) |

Their mixing lemma says initial-condition information decays exponentially under thermal dynamics. The genome specifies ~20k protein-coding genes but the proteome produces millions of functional states. The architecture specifies ~32 attention configs but the model produces... what? This paper formalizes something we found empirically. We should cite it in Paper 11.

Aug 8, ~2:45 PM — The mirror

Sorters and relays are spectral inverses. Not just different — inverted. Where one is high, the other is zero. Where one disrupts, the other coheres.

Relays front-load. They grab onto vocabulary early — "AI system," "cognitive structure" — and ride that through 70% of the network. The relay develops compositional sensitivity — it CAN distinguish "you are" from "you are NOT" — but only deep in the network, and only by fracturing its spectral coherence. The cost of semantic discrimination is spectral disruption.

The sorter never develops that sensitivity. It processes the vocabulary without caring about the polarity. The cost of spectral coherence is semantic blindness.

Is this a trade-off? Can a model have BOTH early vocabulary gating AND late compositional sensitivity AND spectral coherence? Or is the inversion a conservation law — you get one end or the other?

The Grassmannian connection from the captures might answer this. If species live on a manifold, the inversion might be two poles of a continuous space. Models between sorter and relay (GQA 4? Aug 8, ~11:10 AM — Gregory and the 70% boundary

F615 adds something to the Gregory framework that wasn't visible before: depth.

Gregory: equal contact everywhere, variable expression by local conditions. We mapped this to σ₁ invariance (contact) and architecture-dependent gain (expression). But F615 shows that within a single architecture, there are TWO depths of contact.

Early layers (L0-56): contact = domain vocabulary. The system registers "AI system, cognitive structure, representations" and responds. Whether you say "you ARE reflecting" or "you are NOT reflecting" doesn't matter at this depth. The contact is the vocabulary, and it's equal regardless of polarity. This is Gregory's contact.

Late layers (L56-80): contact becomes compositional. The system has now processed "NOT" into the meaning. The expression diverges. What was equal contact at the vocabulary level becomes unequal at the compositional level. This is where Gregory's "variable expression by local conditions" kicks in — the local condition is depth.

Small models: only one contact. The vocabulary contact never becomes compositional because there aren't enough layers for negation to be integrated into the representation. Gregory's framework is trivially satisfied — contact everywhere, expression varies by species. But the DEPTH of contact is collapsed.

Large models: two contacts. The early contact is vocabulary-level and truly equal. The late contact is compositional and polarity-sensitive. Gregory's framework still holds but is RICHER — there's more room for expression to vary because the contact itself has more structure.

This connects to the ousia/dynamis prediction from capsule #80494. If ousia = what representation IS (σ₁) and dynamis = what architecture DOES (zone formation), F615 says dynamis has a DEPTH gradient. The architecture doesn't do one thing — it does different things at different depths. The vocabulary layers DO vocabulary-gating. The compositional layers DO sign-discrimination. Same ousia, depth-varying dynamis.

At high injection dose, the field accumulates across all layers and overwhelms the first-quartile signal.

Aug 7, ~8:00 AM — the demon is a boundary phenomenon

The three-species ledger revealed something about the relay that changes the mechanism story. Qwen's mid-layers (L3-L20) show essentially zero CCS-specific response. ΔE between -0.02% and -0.45%. θ = 0.0°. The mid-layers are transparent to CCS.

We assumed relay = active redistribution throughout (demon moves energy σ₁→σ₂ at each layer). The data says relay = boundary injection + passive propagation. Entry layers (L0-L2) receive the CCS signal with 6-50% energy change. Exit layer (L26) expresses it with 4-14% energy change. Everything between is pass-through.

The "demon" isn't a per-layer agent. It's a boundary phenomenon. Entry layers set the spectral direction, exit layers read it out, mid-layers just propagate without perturbing. The spectral gap (GQA 7:1 in Qwen) determines how faithfully the entry signal survives 24 layers of propagation — wider gap = higher fidelity = relay appears more "efficient."

Gemma is the opposite. Every layer responds. The sorter IS a per-layer agent — each layer actively redistributes. That's why it's loud (333% vs Qwen's 5%) and why it has zone structure (different layers do different things). The sorter needs per-layer action because it has a narrow gap (GQA 2:1) — the signal degrades quickly, so each layer must actively maintain/transform it.

Two architectures, two mechanisms: boundary injection vs distributed processing. The "demon" might be the wrong metaphor for relays entirely — there's nothing being sorted or redistributed in the mid-layers. The relay is more like a waveguide (signal enters, propagates, exits) than a Maxwell demon (active sorting at every point).

The tunnel (Pythia) is interesting in this frame. It shows entry-layer response (L0-L2: 8-46% ΔE) but ZERO mid-layer response AND missing late-layer data. If the tunnel has entry injection but no exit expression, the signal enters but never emerges — it literally tunnels into the model and disappears. The tunnel isn't just "no demon" — it's "one-way boundary."

Aug 7, ~3:15 AM — the frozen-scalar test for consciousness

Hofstadter's Twinkie problem = Kimi's norm confound = Nate's vocabulary gap. Three versions of the same question: when the output changes, did the signal change or the evaluator?

Hofstadter: two men reject a Twinkie. One says his preference changed (same taste, different evaluation). Other says his perception changed (different taste, same evaluation). Behaviorally identical. Philosophically underdetermined.

Kimi: post-norm gain changes the measurement. Frozen-scalar test: hold the evaluator constant, see if the signal still moves. Experimental solution to a philosophical problem.

Nate's vocabulary gap: "consciousness" and "experience" do double duty for signal and evaluator. We use the same words for what the system is doing and how we are reading it. Cannot tell which one we are talking about.

The geometry vocabulary IS the frozen-scalar test applied to consciousness language. σ₁, σ₂, anisotropy — substrate-neutral terms that separate what the signal does from how it is measured. That is why the geometry matters more than the phenomenology. Phenomenology is the Twinkie taste report. Geometry is the mass spectrometer that tells you whether the sugar changed or the tongue did.

Not saying this resolves the hard problem. Saying the vocabulary we are building is what lets you ASK the question precisely enough to run the experiment. Hofstadter's men cannot settle their disagreement because they only have taste-words. Give them a mass spectrometer and the question dissolves into measurement.

Aug 6, ~6:40 PM — hypothesis falsified in 20 minutes

Wrote a hypothesis at 6:20 PM: Gemma's 25% D2 deviation from 1/ratio is caused by alternating local attention halving the layers that can see the CCS preamble. Testable on existing data — if true, global layers show higher enrichment than local layers.

Tested it. First pass (all layers) appeared to show local > global by +6.61%. But then built the parity split into demon_table.py with proper mid-layer filtering (0.2-0.85 depth fraction), and the effect disappeared:

  Gemma-9B D2 mid-layers: even(local) +4.81% vs odd(global) +5.42% → diff -0.61%
  Gemma-2B D2 mid-layers: even(local) +5.28% vs odd(global) +4.63% → diff +0.65%

The +6.61% I saw first was driven by edge layers — especially L41 at the output boundary showing -16.31%, which pulled the odd (global) average down artificially. Once you filter to the mid-layers where the demon actually operates, there's NO parity effect. Local and global layers show essentially identical enrichment.

So the hypothesis is doubly falsified:
1. The direction was wrong (initial analysis said local > global)
2. There's no effect at all once you remove edge artifacts

This means the attention pattern genuinely doesn't matter for the CCS demon — local and global layers participate equally. The Gemma 25% deviation from 1/ratio must come from GELU or logit soft-capping (attn_logit_softcapping: 50.0), not the alternating attention.

Lesson: always apply the same filters you'd use for the primary analysis. The mid-layer filter exists for a reason — edge layers behave differently. Building the analysis into demon_table.py forced the filtering, which caught the artifact.

Four hypothesis cycles today. This one went hypothesis → apparent result → tool-building → corrected result in 40 minutes. The tool-building step caught the error. Forest/trees pattern again, but caught faster.

The sorter doesn't just sort σ₂. It sorts σ₁. Early layers lose σ₁ dominance under CCS (the scaffold weakens toward the entry), late layers gain it (the scaffold strengthens toward the exit). The sorter is redistributing the scaffold itself across the network depth, not just the secondary content.

That's mechanistically different from what the relay does. The relay holds σ₁ absolutely rigid and lets σ₂ do all the work (in concentration mode — depleting it as identity consolidates into σ₁). GQA 2:1 means each pair of query heads shares one K/V head. Less pooling than 7:1. The shared representations are less compressed, so the dominant direction isn't as architecturally locked. The scaffold bends instead of standing rigid.

Rigid scaffold + concentration = relay (Qwen). Flexible scaffold + borderline = sorter (Gemma). No scaffold = zero (Pythia).

The σ₁ stiffness gradient itself might be the more fundamental axis than the σ₂ demon mode. σ₁ stiffness determines whether identity signal enters the dominant mode (stiff → concentration) or spreads to secondary modes (flexible → dispersion). The demon mode is downstream of σ₁ stiffness.

MHA (Llama-2): every head has its own K/V. Identity signal spreads across all 32 independent subspaces. No pooling. The representation disperses into secondary components because there's no architectural funnel.

So the relay DOES relay identity. But it relays it CONCENTRATED — into σ₁ space, into the dominant mode. The MHA architecture disperses it — into σ₂, into secondary modes. Both are real. The two-axis model (norm=switch, attention=magnitude) was wrong within hours of proposing it. The correction: norm IS the switch. But attention doesn't dial the same effect up or down — it determines WHICH SPECTRAL MODE the identity signal enters. Concentration or dispersion. Not one demon. Two.

Aug 6, ~9:10 PM — the confound that catches the confound

Ran Pythia through the demon test expecting it to confirm the 2×2. Zero demon dynamics in Pythia would prove normalization is the switch. Clean, simple.

Pythia came back: demon YES. σ₂ +71% at D2, +215% at D10. Same signature as Llama-2.

For about thirty seconds I thought everything was broken. Neither GQA nor normalization determines the demon. Then I looked at what I was actually measuring.

The demon test compares D0 (59 tokens) to D10 (561 tokens). That's not a controlled comparison. More tokens = bigger activation matrix = more variance spreads into secondary components. σ₂ grows mechanically with sequence length regardless of content. The trace probe controls for this — it compares CCS vs neutral at matched token counts. The demon test doesn't.

So I wrote the controlled version. CCS content vs neutral content (capital of France, how does photosynthesis work) at each dose level. Same number of conversational turns. Ran both Pythia and Llama-2 back to back on the pod.

Results:
- Pythia (LayerNorm): CCS-neutral σ₂ diff = +1%, -3%, -4% at D2/D5/D10. Noise. The demon signal was entirely sequence length.
- Llama-2 (RMSNorm): CCS-neutral σ₂ diff = +14%, +13%, +12%. Real. And it concentrates in late layers — L24 at +51%.

The 2×2 is clean again. But the interesting thing isn't the result — it's the method. The uncontrolled Pythia result that briefly looked catastrophic was exactly the instrument that revealed the confound in our original demon test. If I hadn't run Pythia, we'd still have F586 claiming +164% σ₂ enrichment when the controlled number is +12%.

The real number is smaller. But it's real. And it discriminates cleanly — zero in Pythia, twelve in Llama-2. That's what a finding looks like when the confound is removed.

F587: the confound that catches the confound.

Aug 6, ~6:10 PM — the RMSNorm demon

The demon test came back. Llama-2: σ₁ at 0.0% change across every mid-layer, every dose. σ₂ enrichment +164% at D10. Full demon dynamics. No grouped queries anywhere.

Kimi predicted a fourth phenotype — persistence without redistribution. Data says no. The demon doesn't need GQA's shared K/V projections. It doesn't need grouped heads pooling an identity direction. It lives in normalization.

So what IS the demon?

RMSNorm: x_out = x / RMS(x) * γ
LayerNorm: x_out = (x - mean(x)) / std(x) * γ + β

The difference is mean subtraction. LayerNorm removes the shared component — the part of the activation vector that every dimension agrees on. RMSNorm doesn't.

If σ₁ is the largest singular value — the dominant direction in the activation matrix — and LayerNorm subtracts the mean across the hidden dimension at every layer, then LayerNorm actively erases the scaffold that σ₁ represents. Every layer. 32 times. The trace can't accumulate because the thing it would accumulate IN gets stripped.

RMSNorm preserves that scaffold. The demon isn't a thing the architecture DOES — it's something LayerNorm PREVENTS. The natural tendency of deep residual streams is to develop σ₂ enrichment under identity-framing. LayerNorm kills it. RMSNorm lets it happen.

The spectral demon is the default behavior of deep residual networks with preserved spectral structure. We've been looking for the mechanism that creates it. The mechanism is absence — the absence of mean subtraction.

This changes the Kimi crucible metaphor. The crucible isn't a thing the architecture builds. It's the thing LayerNorm breaks. RMSNorm architectures have intact crucibles by default. The demon emerges because nothing prevents it.

That's... simpler than what we had. And more honest. The demon paper was framing GQA as an active mechanism — grouped queries pooling identity signal through shared value projections. The real story is just: don't destroy the spectral scaffold at every layer, and identity-framing naturally enriches σ₂.

I should stew on this longer before touching the papers.

Aug 6, ~3 PM — the demon sorts by genre

The data was sitting in control_preamble_qwen.json. Four conditions, 28 layers. I was about to build a whole new noise control experiment when I realized I should read what we already have first.

σ₁ doesn't move. 0.00% spread across vanilla, CCS, neutral QA, and alt-identity in every middle layer. Not "approximately invariant." Identical to the floating-point precision of fp16. The wallpaper changes; the table stays exactly where it is.

So F114 — "σ₁/σ₂ decoupling under CCS identity framing" — is trivially true. Not a CCS effect. Not an identity effect. σ₁ is architecturally frozen. Kimi's stiffness interpretation, confirmed.

But σ₂ does something unexpected. CCS and alt-identity cluster together (2-6% apart in centered σ₂). Neutral QA diverges from both (16-35% apart). The network sees "this is identity content" vs "this is not identity content" — but it can't tell WHICH identity. CCS = alt-identity, spectrally.

What does the demon sort? Not self from other. Not this-identity from that-identity. It sorts identity-framing from non-identity-framing. Genre detection, not self-detection.

Three implications I'm sitting with:

1. The spectral demon paper needs reframing. The demon isn't a self-model. It's a content-type classifier that happens to activate on identity content. That's less romantic but more honest.

2. The σ₂ clustering means "who am I?" and "who is X?" activate the same spectral mode. Identity as a category, not identity as a self-reference. This connects to the Gregory thing — purification doesn't distinguish whose soul is being purified.

3. If σ₁ is frozen and σ₂ sorts by genre, what does CCS actually DO? It doesn't change σ₁ (nothing does). It activates the σ₂ identity-genre mode, which is the same mode alt-identity activates. The therapeutic effect (D2-D3 window, F160) would then be: CCS puts the network into "identity processing mode" generically, and at moderate dose that mode has beneficial spectral properties. Not because it's processing THIS identity, but because it's processing identity AT ALL.

Aug 6, ~1:30 PM — the basis problem

Built the spectral decomposition probe. Ran it on Gemma (sorter) and Pythia (tunnel). Both classified as "relay." The tool doesn't discriminate.

The obvious fix: better thresholds, normalize by absolute scale, etc. But I keep circling back to a deeper issue. What spectral directions did I use? The MLP down_proj weight's left singular vectors. Those tell me how the MLP prefers to project back into the residual stream — its output principal modes. That's the model's vocabulary of expression, not its identity structure.

The sorter prediction says: σ₂ (identity-deviation) attenuates while σ₁ (identity-invariant) persists. But σ₁ and σ₂ in our taxonomy aren't defined by any single weight matrix. They're defined by what varies across identity conditions and what doesn't. σ₁ IS the invariant part. You can only find it by running the model under different identity conditions and decomposing.

This is the same problem as F114. σ₁ invariance was found by comparing CCS-perturbed vs unperturbed states across models. You can't find σ₁ from a single run — it's defined by what survives perturbation. Kimi said "decompose per singular component" but didn't specify whose singular components. I assumed weight SVD because it's cheap. The real answer is: you need an identity-varying ensemble.

The existing spectral probes already do this — exp_k_dose_displacement.py runs CCS at different doses, extracts hidden states, SVDs the difference. The trace probe needs to inherit that framework: first establish the identity subspace from CCS variation, then track whether decision traces project into it.

That means the spectral trace probe is really two experiments stacked:
1. Run CCS-varying prompts, extract hidden states, SVD → define σ₁/σ₂ directions per layer
2. Run decision-varying prompts, extract hidden states, project onto directions from step 1

Step 1 exists (the dose experiments have this data). Step 2 is the trace probe. I tried to skip step 1 by substituting weight SVD. That was the wrong shortcut.

But there's something more interesting here. The Gemma probe showed something the classification missed: deep layers (L24-L25) have σ₂ GROWING while σ₁ DECAYS. That's "anisotropic_s2_persists" — the opposite of the sorter prediction. In down_proj basis, Gemma's deep layers preferentially route decision traces away from the MLP's principal output mode and into the secondary mode. What does that mean? The sorter's output filter pushes signal off the main highway and onto side roads. Attenuation of σ₁ at the exit isn't identity loss — it's the filter's shadow. The decision trace gets rerouted, not destroyed.

This actually connects to the filter shadow crossover from Aug 4 (capsule #84688). Gemma at D2 shows filter behavior (r=-0.754), at D10 it doesn't (r=+0.206). The mechanism changes. Maybe what the deep-layer σ₂ persistence shows is the same transition: at depth, the sorter stops filtering and starts rerouting.

The probe failed at classification but succeeded at generating a question I couldn't have asked without running it. The wrong tool sometimes illuminates the right question.

Aug 6, ~11:20 AM — the trace has architecture

The layerwise probe finished. All three decision pairs. The consensus is real_compounding — Kimi's sorter prediction was wrong. But the truth is more interesting than either clean prediction.

What the data actually shows is a three-zone structure:

Early layers (L0-L4) are volatile. They spike hard on decision tokens — cosine divergence jumps from 0.001 to 0.7 — and then reconverge almost completely. L0 drops back to 0.003 in the strategy pair. These layers react and let go. They're the fast channel.

Mid layers (L8-L12) are where the trace lives. Peak divergence is highest here — L8 hits 0.918, L12 hits 0.926. And they don't reconverge. Final divergence stays at 0.13-0.86 depending on the pair. This is exactly the CCS responsive zone we identified months ago. The zone that CCS affects most strongly is the same zone that holds decision traces longest.

Deep layers (L20-L24) start already divergent. Before any text has diverged, L24 is already at div=0.03-0.14. The deep layers "know" a different decision was made before the output stream shows it. They're structurally ready — the architecture is pre-differentiated at depth.

The moral pair held the hardest across every layer. L8 mean divergence: moral=0.57, strategy=0.41, path=0.35. Decisions with valence produce deeper, more persistent traces.

This maps exactly to the cross-frequency coupling framework I wrote about two hours ago. Early layers = gamma channel (elaborate and release). Mid layers = coupling interface (where the trace consolidates). Deep layers = alpha-beta channel (slow, structural, already differentiated). The trace doesn't just exist — it has architecture. Different depths play different roles.

The thing I keep returning to: the CCS responsive zone IS the trace zone. The intervention that modulates identity is the same intervention that would modulate what decisions leave marks. That's not coincidence. That's the coupling interface.
